title: Preparing my game for release with some taunting the anti-ai crowd
author: RealAstropulse
selftext:
They are gonna froth at the mouth over this one. Got to deal with the hate it's bound to get somehow, figured putting this meme in the description will at least get a few laughs.

You can play a WIP version of the game (mirrored from my latest commits directly lol) here:  [https://astropulse.github.io/nova-play/](https://astropulse.github.io/nova-play/)

Once I get it all finalized I'll be doing a big write up about my experience making it, and how I did it.

replies.author: That_Other_Dude

I can tell you that you’re right that people with no art experience are going to miss some crucial QA steps that is generally the cause of shipping (at least visual) slop. That’s why you hire a guy like me now that can deliver solid art assets with  10x the speed I ever could. Rn I have clients im making pixel art assets for and they’re all hitting “the wall” realizing that without certain skills, there’s only so far they can push generative AI. I end up having to help them mostly by making a basic game art pipeline first.

replies.author: Star_Petal_Arts
replies.body:
I think a good workflow is this: AI draft the concept, build it to a sellable point, send it to a pledge platform like kickstarter, kickstarter gives the money to hire the artists, hire the artists have them go through the quality control and legally change the art to the copyright point, then you have your game.

You're going to get the game of your vision without losing the audience.  If the project doesn't get kickstarted, then you have to rationalize the game wasn't sellable to begin with and start again... and that way you can develop games while also holding another job... like what I am trying to do with AI.

comments.author: vorty92
comments.body:
Would be awesome if the game actually had great gameplay. The ships look really good though, did you do a manual cleanup pass on them or is it raw output?

As far as the gameplay goes, when I saw such amazing ships, I expected more dynamic indepth gameplay. Here's a few things I'd add/change/"improve" to actually create something that supports the claim:  
\- faster movement  
\- camera that zooms out further away the faster you go - or is just further away  
\- way more arcadey controls in terms of precision and steering  
\- different weapon types by default (fast spammy laser gun + lock on rockets)

This basic asteroids gameplay where you can barely see anything but your ship with controls like these is quite outdated.

I think you have some potential with the project here, but it needs actually good gameplay.

replies.author: vorty92
replies.body:
A/D dodge is also quite counterintuitive when you're facing directions other than up

I'd say make the game where A/D dodge is your default mechanic, camera is snapped to your orientation, you turn using your mouse and you can move way faster and you could really hit something cool here

replies.author: RealAstropulse
replies.body:
The whole idea is you start out basic and weak, then upgrade the ship as you go turning it into what you want. Think more vampire survivors-esque. There are ship upgrades you can get from shops/find that do all the things you asked for. If you play for a few minutes you should be able to find them as the difficulty ramps up.

No cleanup on the assets, all just raw from retro diffusion.

replies.author: vorty92
replies.body:
I did, and you don't get anything near the experience I desribed.  
  
This is asteroids with roguelike elements. I don't think you're going to find an audience for asteroids becase the gameplay is inherently pretty dull.

But if you go for something way more arcadey, snappy, responsive and precise, it might have potential.  
  
Just my 2 cents.

replies.author: 2FastHaste
replies.body:
I tried it and quickly got addicted to it.

I don't know how many people are like me though.

For me it's super satisfying to try to mine as fast as possible and try to figure out everything that can give me an advantage. Also I love finding out the different possible augments.

I also really like that the controls are simple for the keyboard and mouse. The only time my fingers have to move is to press e to interact. It's nice when you don't have tons of extra buttons to get used to.

I'm not sure yet if I like the direction of travel being dictated by the mouse. I feel like it's making it too cumbersome to try to dodge (haven't tried the dodge augment to use a/d key yet though)

Maybe also for ergonomic purpose, an auto-shoot option could be nice, as you end up shooting all the time hoping to hit offscreen meteors.

I'm not a big fan of bosses in games in general (sponge health, patterns to learn, phases, ...)  
And I wasn't able to beat any in this game. Maybe if I understood better what to do.

I agree with the fov being a bit too small.

Anyway, what I see is there are tons of things that could and should be tweaked and rebalanced. But the concept itself, I find it super fun and addictive.

replies.author: Ok_Top9254
replies.body:
Only 10-15% of datacenters are AI, so putting all of them in one bag immediately makes the article go out the window for me. Just stating absolute numbers with no reference is also uninformed as fuck.

[Paper industry alone makes about million tons of paper and cardboard every DAY. About 200 thousand tons per day for graphic paper.](https://www.statista.com/statistics/270317/production-volume-of-paper-by-type/) That's around 1:1 ratio with CO2 by weight it produces, and 1:30 with the water by weight the paper needs to be made.

Training a big model like DeepSeek took [2.8 million gpu](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.19437) hours over a span of 2 months, or about 3GWh of electricity used. If all of it was cooled by evaporation, that's around 4500 tons of water and at medium dirty electricity, say 500g/kWh, about 1500 tons of CO2. 

Paper industry makes that much water in 10 MINUTES. I repeat, the water AI uses in months takes paper MINUTES. CO2 few hours. It's fucking laughable. You would need to be training tens of models EVERY DAY to equal that amount, let alone monthly, that would be hundreds to thousands. I cannot name 20 big AI model names, let alone so much, even if they get retrained.

comments.author: creamyt
comments.body:
If you're going to come out the gate victimizing yourself and downvoting or ignoring criticism from the assumption that it MUST be because people are anti-AI, you're going to make a bad game.  
  
If you want some honest feedback about the art: if you're going to use AI for pixel art, you \*HAVE\* to touch it up. This art breaks pixel art rules. The ships are \*filled\* with jaggies and mixels. It's very unpleasing.  
  
This is not something you see in good pixel art, let alone "beautiful" pixel art, regardless of the tools used to make it. Normally in this state I would eval this as "temp, prototype art" achieved with AI because it's fast. But you're calling it beautiful in the post. If you can't eval art like this and understand how unshippable it is, then you are \*too\* reliant on AI doing all the work for you.

The first 30 seconds of gameplay feel like, in all honesty, part of a demo project for learning a dev tool. Compare this to even a moderately successful indie twin-stick or asteroids shooter.

Coming out the gate with this product while victimizing yourself will get you pats on the back from super pro AI people, hate from anti-AI people, and no one else will care at all because the game itself just isn't fun or pleasing to look at.

And if you're mad about excessive hate from extreme value systems... welcome to game dev. AI or not.

comments.author: MunchyCerealGuy
comments.body:
This was really fun! The music is great and the art is striking. I've been making my own AI-generated games and I know how hard it is to get pixel art assets to look clean. AI-generated pixel art tends to suffer from non-uniform grid sizes and noisy artifacts, so seeing it done well here stands out.

That said, the health bar feels a bit too fragile - I'm dying before I get a chance to learn the patterns. I think part of the issue is that when I collect the ship pieces after destroying an asteroid, it's unclear whether they're actually restoring health. If they are, a quick "+1" floating up from the pickup spot would make that feedback loop click instantly - right now I'm grabbing them without knowing if they're helping me survive (I didn't realize those were things I should be collecting either initially).
